summary.text: Writing \(\zeta(n)\) and \(\zeta(2n)\) as Dirichlet series, the proof isolates the terms through bases 10 and 3 respectively; after clearing the positive denominator and rewriting composite-base terms as products, the leading terms cancel and every remaining finite monomial is \(O(11^{-n})\). The residual tails are bounded by comparison with a shifted inverse-square series, and \(\zeta(n)^2+\zeta(2n)\ge 2\), yielding an explicit error bound \(725\cdot 11^{-n}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
t(n)=\frac{\zeta(2n)}{\zeta(n)^2}
\]
for positive integers \(n>1\). We prove the stronger quantitative assertion that, for every integer \(n\ge 4\),
\[
\left|\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}-
 \left(2^{-n}+3^{-n}+5^{-n}+7^{-n}\right)\right|
 \le 725\,11^{-n}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
The claimed asymptotic formula follows immediately from this uniform estimate.

We first record a tail estimate that will be used twice. For integers \(m\ge 1\) and \(q\ge 0\),
\[
\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac1{k^{q+2}}
 \le \frac{m^2}{m^{q+2}}\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac1{k^2}
 \le \frac{2m^2}{m^{q+2}}.                               \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, for \(k\ge m\), we have \(k^q\ge m^q\), and hence
\[
\frac1{k^{q+2}}\le \frac1{m^q}\frac1{k^2}
=\frac{m^2}{m^{q+2}}\frac1{k^2}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}k^{-2}\le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{6}<2,
\]
which proves (2). Non-strict inequalities with the constant \(2\) will be enough below.

Fix from now on an integer \(n\ge 4\), and introduce the abbreviations
\[
x=2^{-n},\qquad y=3^{-n},\qquad z=5^{-n},\qquad w=7^{-n},
\qquad L=11^{-n}.
\]
Set
\[
g=x+y+z+w                                                   \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
h=x^2+xy+x^3+y^2+xz.                                      \tag{4}
\]
All of these quantities are nonnegative. Also
\[
0\le w\le z\le y\le x.
\]
Since \(n\ge4\),
\[
x=2^{-n}\le 2^{-4}=\frac1{16}.
\]
In particular, \(x\le 1/4\), and therefore
\[
0\le g\le4x\le1.                                         \tag{5}
\]

For \(n>1\), the usual absolutely convergent Dirichlet series for the zeta function gives
\[
\zeta(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-n},\qquad
\zeta(2n)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-2n}.                    \tag{6}
\]
We split the first series after \(10\) and the second after \(3\). Define
\[
T=\sum_{k=11}^{\infty}k^{-n},\qquad
U=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}k^{-2n}.                            \tag{7}
\]
The terms from \(1\) through \(10\) in the first series can be expressed in terms of \(x,y,z,w\):
\[
4^{-n}=x^2,\quad 6^{-n}=xy,\quad 8^{-n}=x^3,
\quad 9^{-n}=y^2,\quad 10^{-n}=xz.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\zeta(n)=1+g+h+T.                                         \tag{8}
\]
Likewise, \(2^{-2n}=x^2\) and \(3^{-2n}=y^2\), so
\[
\zeta(2n)=1+x^2+y^2+U.                                   \tag{9}
\]
For convenience put
\[
P=1+g+h,\qquad Q=1+x^2+y^2,
\]
so that \(\zeta(n)=P+T\) and \(\zeta(2n)=Q+U\).

We next bound the tails. Applying (2) with \(m=11\) and \(q=n-2\) gives
\[
0\le T\le 2\cdot11^2\,11^{-n}=242L.                     \tag{10}
\]
Applying (2) with \(m=4\) and \(q=2n-2\) gives
\[
0\le U\le 2\cdot4^2\,4^{-2n}=32\,16^{-n}\le32L,         \tag{11}
\]
because \(16^{-n}\le11^{-n}\).

We shall also need the rough bounds \(P\le2\) and \(T\le1\). Clearly \(P\ge1\). Every one of \(x,y,z,w\) is at most \(x\). Also, because \(0\le x,y,z\le1\) and \(y,z\le x\), each of the five terms \(x^2,xy,x^3,y^2,xz\) is at most \(x\). Hence
\[
g+h\le9x\le\frac9{16}<1,
\]
and thus
\[
1\le P\le2.                                               \tag{12}
\]
Furthermore, \(242\le11^4\le11^n\), so (10) yields
\[
0\le T\le1.                                               \tag{13}
\]

The main point is now an explicit cancellation in the finite parts of the two zeta series. We first list the elementary monomial estimates that will control all terms remaining after cancellation. Since a product such as \(xw\) equals \((2\cdot7)^{-n}\), and since \(c^{-n}\le11^{-n}=L\) whenever \(c\ge11\), we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
xw&=14^{-n}\le L,& yz&=15^{-n}\le L,& yw&=21^{-n}\le L,\\
z^2&=25^{-n}\le L,& zw&=35^{-n}\le L,& w^2&=49^{-n}\le L,\\
x^2y&=12^{-n}\le L,& xy^2&=18^{-n}\le L,& x^4&=16^{-n}\le L.
\end{aligned}                                             \tag{14}
\]

Consider the finite-part expression
\[
M_{\rm fin}=(1-g)P^2-(1+g)Q
=(1-g)(1+g+h)^2-(1+g)(1+x^2+y^2).                         \tag{15}
\]
A direct expansion and collection of like terms gives the identity
\[
M_{\rm fin}=-W-2g^2h+(1-g)h^2,                            \tag{16}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
W={}&2xw+2yz+2yw+(z+w)^2\\
&+(y+z+w)(g^2+gx+2x^2)+gy^2.                              \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]
For completeness, this identity follows simply by substituting
\(g=x+y+z+w\), \(h=x^2+xy+x^3+y^2+xz\), expanding both sides, and cancelling. Its significance is that terms of sizes \(x,y,z,w\), and all other monomials whose associated base is below \(11\), have disappeared.

We now bound the three pieces in (16). First,
\[
(z+w)^2=z^2+2zw+w^2\le4L.                                \tag{18}
\]
Since \(y+z+w\le3y\), \(g\le4x\), and all quantities are nonnegative,
\[
g^2+gx+2x^2\le16x^2+4x^2+2x^2=22x^2.
\]
It follows from (14) that
\[
(y+z+w)(g^2+gx+2x^2)
 \le 3y\cdot22x^2=66x^2y\le66L.                          \tag{19}
\]
Similarly,
\[
gy^2\le4xy^2\le4L.                                     \tag{20}
\]
Combining (14), (18), (19), and (20), and remembering the coefficients of the first three terms in (17), gives
\[
0\le W\le(2+2+2+4+66+4)L=80L.                            \tag{21}
\]

Next, every term in \(h\) is nonnegative and at most \(x^2\): indeed, \(xy\le x^2\), \(x^3\le x^2\), \(y^2\le x^2\), and \(xz\le x^2\). Thus
\[
0\le h\le5x^2.                                           \tag{22}
\]
Together with \(g\le4x\), this gives
\[
0\le2g^2h\le2(4x)^2(5x^2)=160x^4\le160L.                \tag{23}
\]
Finally, by (5), \(0\le1-g\le1\), and hence
\[
0\le(1-g)h^2\le25x^4\le25L.                             \tag{24}
\]
The expression in (16) is therefore bounded below by
\(-80L-160L=-240L\), while it is bounded above by \(25L\). In particular,
\[
|M_{\rm fin}|\le240L.                                    \tag{25}
\]

It remains to account for the tails \(T\) and \(U\). Expanding \((P+T)^2\) gives the exact decomposition
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(1-g)(P+T)^2-(1+g)(Q+U)\\
&\qquad=M_{\rm fin}+E,                                   \tag{26}
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
E=(1-g)(2PT+T^2)-(1+g)U.                                 \tag{27}
\]
By (5), (12), and (13),
\[
0\le2PT+T^2\le4T+T=5T.
\]
Thus
\[
0\le(1-g)(2PT+T^2)\le5T\le1210L.                        \tag{28}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
0\le(1+g)U\le2U\le64L.                                  \tag{29}
\]
The two terms in (27) have opposite signs. Equations (28) and (29) therefore imply
\[
|E|\le\max(1210L,64L)=1210L.                             \tag{30}
\]
Combining (25), (26), and (30), we obtain
\[
\left|(1-g)\zeta(n)^2-(1+g)\zeta(2n)\right|
 \le1450L.                                                \tag{31}
\]

We finally translate this numerator estimate into the desired ratio estimate. Since all terms in the zeta series are nonnegative and the first term is \(1\),
\[
\zeta(n)\ge1,\qquad \zeta(2n)\ge1.
\]
In particular,
\[
D:=\zeta(n)^2+\zeta(2n)\ge2>0.                            \tag{32}
\]
Using \(t(n)=\zeta(2n)/\zeta(n)^2\) and the positivity of \(\zeta(n)\), ordinary fraction arithmetic gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}-g
&=\frac{1-\zeta(2n)/\zeta(n)^2}
        {1+\zeta(2n)/\zeta(n)^2}-g\\
&=\frac{(1-g)\zeta(n)^2-(1+g)\zeta(2n)}
        {\zeta(n)^2+\zeta(2n)}.                          \tag{33}
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking absolute values in (33), then applying (31) and (32), yields
\[
\left|\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}-g\right|
\le \frac{1450L}{2}=725L.
\]
Recalling \(g=2^{-n}+3^{-n}+5^{-n}+7^{-n}\) and \(L=11^{-n}\), this is exactly (1).

Thus, for all \(n\ge4\), the difference between the left-hand side and the four displayed inverse powers is bounded in absolute value by \(725\cdot11^{-n}\). By the definition of big-O along the positive integers, this proves
\[
\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}
=\frac1{2^n}+\frac1{3^n}+\frac1{5^n}+\frac1{7^n}
+O(11^{-n})
\qquad(n\to\infty).
\]
